analysis.one_liner: Exempts power plant efficiency, pollution-control, and grid-reliability upgrades from Clean Air Act permitting review.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Clean Air Act's 'new source review' rules, which require power plants and other big polluters to get approval before making major modifications that can increase emissions. It would carve out three categories of projects — energy efficiency projects, pollution control projects, and electric grid reliability projects — from that review entirely. Plant operators would no longer need a permit for those changes, even for projects done in groups during the same outage. The measure never moved past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of power plants and other large industrial facilities, especially older coal-fired plants, gain by avoiding the time, cost, and legal exposure of Clean Air Act permitting for modification projects. The bill was introduced by three members from Virginia and West Virginia, states where coal-fired generation is a major industry.

how_it_helps.text: The bill excludes energy efficiency projects, pollution control projects, and reliability projects from the 'new source review' process that requires stationary air pollution sources to get approval before construction or modification.

An energy efficiency project is defined as one that lowers the source's maximum hourly carbon dioxide emissions rate, with other regulated pollutants allowed to rise up to the facility's permitted emission rate without triggering review.

Reliability projects are defined to include work that helps the electric grid withstand sudden disturbances including manmade physical or cyber attacks, so utilities could make such changes without permits.

analysis.who_pays: Communities living near power plants, who lose a formal review step that currently documents and limits emissions changes at their local facilities. Federal and state air regulators also lose a tool for scrutinizing project-by-project changes; enforcement falls back on the plant staying within existing permit limits.

drawbacks.text: Under the bill's own definitions, a qualifying 'energy efficiency project' can allow a plant's maximum hourly emissions of pollutants other than carbon dioxide to rise up to its permitted rate without any new source review — so neighbors' exposure to smog-forming or toxic pollutants could increase with no review.

A 'pollution control project' is defined as any project undertaken to reduce emissions of any pollutant; combined with the exemption for groups of changes made during the same outage period, this gives operators a broad category that could shield other simultaneous changes from permitting.

Supporters argue the opposite case: that new source review is slow and costly, and that the threat of triggering it discourages plants from making efficiency upgrades that would actually cut emissions — the bill's stated purpose is to remove that deterrent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument that permitting requirements can deter genuine efficiency upgrades, and projects that cut carbon dioxide emissions have real value. But the bill is drawn broadly: it waives review for any project claimed to reduce any pollutant, and its efficiency definition allows other pollutants to rise to permitted levels unchecked. The main financial effect is to save plant owners permitting costs and litigation risk, while the public's assurance shifts entirely to existing permit limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 29, 2017 by Rep. H. Morgan Griffith, along with Reps. David McKinley and Evan Jenkins of West Virginia.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history for the remainder of the 115th Congress.
Eighteen Republican representatives cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Power plant operators are better off because the bill never passed: they kept operating under the existing new source review rules. People living near industrial facilities also benefit from the unchanged permitting baseline.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plant operators, who kept facing permitting

for.name: Rep. H. Morgan Griffith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt efficiency, pollution-control, and reliability projects from Clean Air Act modification review.

for.name: Reps. David McKinley and Evan Jenkins
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill on its first day.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Greg Walden, R)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat in a committee chaired by a Republican without action, so no party opposed it on the record.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and electric utilities
industries.note: The bill would spare plant operators the cost and delay of Clean Air Act permitting for modifications labeled as efficiency, pollution-control, or reliability projects. The savings come from removing a review step that protects the air quality of neighboring communities; the operators' interest here runs against that protection.

industries.industry: Environmental permitting, testing, and consulting firms
industries.note: Fewer projects triggering new source review would mean less paid permitting work for consultants who prepare applications and modeling for utilities. Their loss tracks with the public losing the review itself.
